The are some very real costs to JavaScript frameworks. These frameworks do not exist to empower developers. They exist to:

* so that employers do not have to invest in training developers.

* to ease candidate selection at hiring, which greases the wheels of hiring/firing

In the big corporate world, especially at non-software companies, there is a culture that strongly believes internally written software sucks. This is Invented Here syndrome, and it reflects that internal developers cannot write software and employers will not invest in maintenance.

The larger costs there are human costs, the inability to efficiently solve any problem outside the constraints imposed by the framework.

> Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc.

Yes, of course they asked.

The agents responded with how this framework is X, not Y. How creating it was a sharp commentary on other frameworks. A couple honest caveats, and a succinct bottom line that adequately kissed the user's ass.

Besides a rewrite to another framework using AI, another option is to modernize the framework with AI instead. Personally, I started to like Mithril after having worked with it for a few years. Instead of rewriting it to a better maintained alternative (mithril doesn't have much active development going on since 2015), I used agents to add signals, proper state management, typing, ssr, computed properties, Bun tooling and more to it. Thanks to the existing test suite, changes landed quite reliably. Source: https://code.garage44.eu/jeroen/mithril

This is buried at the end.

> My goal here is not to write the end-all-be-all benchmark for “I’m a vibe-coder, which framework should I choose?” The point of this post is to demonstrate that it’s possible in the era of AI coding to still make decisions based on evidence rather than vibes.

But it’s obvious that the article will be understood as a useful benchmark, so author probably should have addressed that point earlier and more thoroughly.

Taking the authors pov for a moment, they just showed you how to put all your criticisms to work in making a newer better benchmark :)

It's astonishing to me that even after a decade of SPA frameworks, most authors don't understand how a browser engine like Chrome works. There's enormous cost of manipulating the DOM from JS, as HTML elements get bound to JS objects lazily.

An actual high performance framework should manipulate HTML as a string directly, or through HTML templates (another feature that has existed in most browsers for a decade).

If you're not building a complex application on top of the web stack (interestingly these increasingly use WASM and their own GUI frameworks, so another moot point), but building an interactive consumption website (scrollable lists of static contents), I'd say instead of fronted frameworks, what most people actually would need is Chrome's experimental declarative partial updates:

https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/declarative-p...

Which basically stream HTML fragments from the web.

This benchmark is too simplified to be meaningful. The choice of a framework is rarely based on speed alone, it factors in other elements like the user's domain knowledge, long term maintainability and the framework's track record itself w.r.t security and development of features.

In this regard alone, it will make a lot of sense to spend extra $2 and 2 mins to trade off for a long-term maintainable codebase and code you can reason about than just something made quickly just to get it deployed fast.

In my personal use case, that would be Svelte 5 for me and I'm sure it will be something else for everyone.
Astro comes out on top with the best time, #2 lowest spend and zero client side JS. I know what I'm using for my next project.

This experiment could be reframed as: which framework's abstractions are best suited to building "the Pokémon app."

The results might differ if you were building Facebook, or Instagram, or X, or a static web page for the local coffee shop ...

There will always be trade-offs, but tailoring your abstractions to the project is usually a better decision than not doing so.

Communication has lately proven itself to be as important as ever. If your team has to approve and maintain the result, then using abstractions the team already knows could be the difference between approving the PR today and mythical-man-monthing yourselves as release-blocking capacity -- yet-to-be-onboarded -- for a project that only the AI understands.

I enjoyed reading this article. I think it's an important article. Even though people might disagree about certain definitions like "maintainability," I liked what the author did by sticking to objective measurements which do correlate somewhat with the things we care about: Ability to implement the product fast, with few tokens and with as few lines of code as possible in the final product. These are well chosen metrics IMO.

Fewer lines of code (per piece of functionality) does, in fact, correlate strongly with maintainability. The downside of this metric to watch out for (as Goodhart's Law would have it) is to ensure that the framework isn't compromising (current or future) flexibility in an unacceptable way. I imagine if this kind of benchmark becomes popular, people would start coming up with low code frameworks which are extremely rigid and inflexible. Because rigidity is a good way to cut lines of code. There needs to be a way to ascertain the flexibility limits of the framework too.

Would be good to have a similar benchmark for a more complex application; one with authentication, access control (with individual ownership of records and group ownership).

Also would be good to compare the security of different frameworks in this way. See which frameworks leave security gaps. Would be good to set up a benchmark where an AI agent is made to impersonate different users (with different roles) and test access to all possible data types and views in an exhaustive way.

A while ago, I showed Claude a relatively complex application I had built with my framework https://saasufy.com/ and asked it to estimate how many lines of code and how long would be required to build the same application with a stack like React + Node.js + Postgres and it estimated that it would require 4 to 5 times the amount of code and amount of time so I'm keen to actually test it out with a benchmark like this.

I was not surprised that HTMX lead in a lot of the benchmarks. I suspect it would do even better with a more complex application. IMO, its design is closer in spirit to where the industry needs to go. There are a lot of maintainability and security gains to be had by standardizing frontend and backend interactions; though I believe there are other way to do this which can yield even more gains (though obviously with some tradeoffs depending on the use case).

The point of using a framework is to reduce mental load at expense of customizability. The moment you need to change something in the framework - this mental model falls apart.

Obvious solutions are to vendor your dependencies (compile the framework from owned source) or to drop to the lower level of abstraction.

LLMs should have no problem using browser/node APIs directly since they're very well used, well documented, and not changing as much as higher level software does.

my experience is that one-shotting a simple front end works great. Then you want to add features and move things around and each turn starts getting slower and the single page with JS and CSS and HTML starts to turn into a 3000 line monster and your context window starts to creak under the strain of even simple changes, because the LLM has to keep more and more of the application in its head just to make relatively small changes without breaking something else. Either you should have started with some kind of framework with hygienic rules on how to separate concerns or at minimum a good set of coding standards that force the LLM to start building clean components from scratch. The benefit isn't necessarily cleaner code for its own sake, it's that the LLM can work on one part of the application without having to understand the whole thing every time. That being said, once you have a 3000 line prototype it's not that complex to simply ask the LLM to refactor it into a set of orthogonal components. As long as it was building unit tests using playwright or something this can turn your slop into framework code cleanly. The interesting question is whether you saved anything by putting off that structure in the first place.

Even today with React and Opus 5.5 it couldn't match the development performance of version 2.

That said, both are "fast enough" and if you're on an enterprise plan, the cost difference is neglible. I waste way more more tokens due to poor or imprecise requirements than I do on development.

Models are trained on existing frameworks, so they don't have to hold it all in their context to reason about it; it's baked into the weights. Same goes for the humans reviewing the code. I don't see the benefit of writing your own framework for most companies.
